content: The General Practitioner (GP) contract has undergone changes, with performance now assessed through the Quality and Outcomes Framework. This framework evaluates factors such as the number of patients treated, the types of treatments administered, and the overall health outcomes of the GP's catchment area. GPs are encouraged to prescribe medications using their generic names to promote cost-effectiveness. The IT system used to calculate GP income based on these criteria is known as QMAS (Quality Management and Analysis System). A GP in the UK can expect to earn approximately £70,000 annually without working overtime, although this figure can vary significantly. Recent reports suggest that some GPs have the potential to earn as much as £250,000 per year, a figure that has drawn criticism in the media for being excessive. However, the average full-time GP now earns around £110,000 before tax. Despite this, many GPs earn significantly less and are required to work inconvenient and unsociable hours, such as attending to patients during personal events like children's birthday parties on weekends. GP practices have faced criticism for a perceived lack of accountability, particularly in handling complaints. A recent report highlighted failures in the NHS complaints system to identify issues of professional misconduct or criminal activity. While complaint procedures have been tightened, there is growing concern that malicious complaints and unrealistic patient expectations are contributing to increased stress levels among GPs. As independent contractors, GP practices have discretion in how they operate. Primary Care Trusts cannot intervene in complaints until the practice has addressed them, and patients risk being removed from a GP's list if conflicts arise. In Ireland, the structure of general practice closely mirrors the UK model, with some differences. To become a GP in Ireland, one must first complete a primary medical degree, typically a 5to 6-year undergraduate program at one of the country's five medical schools. Graduates are awarded the title MB BCh BAO (Doctor of Medicine, Doctor of Surgery, and Doctor of Obstetrics and Gynaecology). Following this, a one-year internship is required, during which trainees rotate through medical and surgical specialties, often spending six months in each. Some interns may also gain experience in general practice, psychiatry, or other specialties. Successful completion of the internship leads to full registration with the Irish Medical Council. Doctors wishing to pursue a career in general practice must complete an approved training scheme. Previously, it was not mandatory to complete such a scheme to sit the MICGP (Member of the Irish College of General Practitioners) exam and practice as a GP in Ireland. Many doctors opted for standalone Senior House Officer (SHO) posts in the required specialties and then sat the exam without vocational training. However, vocational training is now mandatory. While alternative routes, such as the MRCGP (Membership of the Royal College of General Practitioners), remain possible, Irish-trained GPs are often at a significant advantage when applying for GP positions in Ireland. Entry into a General Practice Training Scheme is highly competitive and typically involves an interview process. Most schemes last four years, with one extending to five years. The first two years are generally spent rotating through relevant specialties, such as medicine, paediatrics, obstetrics and gynaecology, psychiatry, accident and emergency, and ENT (ear, nose, and throat). The final two years are spent as a GP registrar in a designated training practice. Upon successfully completing the MICGP exams, the new general practitioner is free to practice independently. General practice in Ireland is a highly desirable career, and competition for training places is intense. There has been significant criticism regarding the perceived undersupply of training positions, and efforts are being made to increase the number of places annually. Currently, there are 12 training schemes across Ireland, including Donegal, Sligo, Western (Galway, Mayo, and Roscommon), Mid-Western (Limerick, Clare, and North Tipperary), Southern (Cork and Kerry), South-East (Waterford, Wexford, Kilkenny, and South Tipperary), Midlands (Offaly, Westmeath, Laois, and Kildare), North-East (Louth, Meath, Monaghan, and Cavan), Ballinasloe, and three schemes based in Dublin. GPs in Ireland may treat patients on a fee-for-service basis, a mix of public and private patients, or exclusively public patients. Public patients are those who qualify for a medical card under the General Medical Services (GMS) system, which provides free healthcare funded by the government. Eligibility for a medical card is means-tested, although certain groups, such as individuals with specific chronic illnesses and the elderly, are also entitled to one. A medical card grants the holder free GP consultations, medications, and hospital treatment. To treat medical card holders, a GP must apply for and be granted a GMS list. These lists are highly competitive, as they can be very lucrative, and vacancies are rare. GPs manage a wide range of medical conditions, making them well-positioned to implement preventative measures and manage chronic illnesses. They also serve as gatekeepers to the tertiary care system, providing referrals to specialist services when necessary. Some GPs are employed by private agencies, further diversifying their roles within the healthcare system.
